cl_dc_pill_logo.q: Can a pill's logo or look tell you what's in it?
cl_dc_pill_logo.short: Nobody has shown it can. In a Dutch check, about 40 in 100 online pill reports claimed over 10 mg more MDMA than lab tests found in matching pills.
cl_dc_pill_logo.but: Nobody has measured how much pills with the same logo differ. And the online check is one Dutch study of two websites.
how: Staff of the Dutch testing service compared 471 online reports about ecstasy pills from 2014–15 with lab results for pills matching each description. About 40 in 100 said over 10 mg too much MDMA, 18 in 100 over 10 mg too little, and 16 in 100 missed another drug.

The authors called 15 in 100 reports dangerous: far too little MDMA, or a drug left out. Saying too much wasn't counted. A photo helped find the right pill but didn't make reports less often dangerous. Reports giving a range were dangerous less often: 12 against 21 in 100.

The same testers say pills that looked like ecstasy, with similar logos, have held 2C-B or amphetamine. They identify some pills by exact size, weight, logo and a colour test, against pills tested in recent weeks. They call it 99% reliable but have published no data.

In lab tests of Dutch pills sold as ecstasy from 1993 to 2008, only MDMA was found in 44 in 100 in 1997 and about 86 in 100 in 2000–04. Single pills held from a trace to 225 mg. These are lab amounts, not amounts to take.
cl_dc_pill_logo.rate: One Dutch study of two websites, by the team that runs the lab records it checked against. Nobody measured how much pills with the same logo differ, and the '99% reliable' figure has no published data.

drug-checking.statement: An online pill report with a photo is more likely to be right.
drug-checking.why: In a Dutch check against lab tests, a photo helped match a report to the right pill. But reports with photos were not less often dangerously wrong: far too little MDMA, or a drug left out.

mdma.statement: Online pill reports more often claim too much MDMA than too little.
mdma.why: Checked against Dutch lab tests in 2014–15, about 40 in 100 reports said over 10 mg too much and 18 in 100 over 10 mg too little. That's two websites in one country.
